typical_mindset: In a pictograph where one symbol stands for several units (e.g. 1 symbol = 10 books), the number of symbols itself is reported as the answer instead of multiplying by what each symbol represents — the scale/key of the pictograph is overlooked, and the count of pictures is treated as the count of the real quantity.
explanation_strategy: Point back at the key first and ask what one symbol is worth, before asking the child to work out the total for a row — make the multiplication step explicit rather than assumed.

example_dialogue.text: The key says one symbol stands for 10 books. If a row has 3 symbols, how many books is that?
Each symbol is worth 10 books, not 1 — so how many books do 3 symbols really stand for?

typical_mindset: A bar's height is read by eye against the nearest gridline rather than tracing carefully to the exact value the bar's top actually reaches — when a bar falls between two gridlines, the child rounds to whichever gridline looks closest rather than reading the precise value intended.
explanation_strategy: Have the child place a finger exactly at the top of the bar and then trace straight across to the number scale, rather than estimating by eye, so the read-off is anchored to the bar's true top edge.

example_dialogue.text: Put your finger right at the very top of this bar. Now trace straight across to the numbers on the side — what number does your finger land on?
It's right between 30 and 40... closer to 35.
Good noticing — that's the real value, even though it's not exactly on a gridline.

typical_mindset: When a question asks for a combined total across several categories (e.g. 'how many books were sold in all three months'), the child instead reports just the single largest category's value — as if 'in all' meant 'pick out the biggest one' rather than 'add every one together.'
explanation_strategy: Ask the child to name each category's value out loud one at a time, then ask what 'in all' or 'altogether' means to do with a list of separate numbers, before reaching for one number as the answer.

example_dialogue.text: What were the three months' values — January, February, March?
Good. The question asks for the total 'in all three months' — does that mean picking the biggest one, or combining all three?
